content: MT-TD, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA aspartic acid, is a transfer RNA molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TD gene in humans. The MT-TD gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 67 base pairs. The structure of a tRNA molecule is characterized by a unique folded configuration that includes three hairpin loops, resembling a three-leafed clover. The MT-TD gene encodes a small transfer RNA (mapped to human mitochondrial DNA positions 7518–7585) that facilitates the transfer of the amino acid aspartic acid to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during protein synthesis, specifically during the translation process. Mutations in the MT-TD gene have been linked to complex IV deficiency of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, also referred to as cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. This is a rare genetic disorder that can affect multiple organ systems, including skeletal muscles, the heart, the brain, and the liver. Clinical manifestations of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency commonly include myopathy, hypotonia, encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. One patient with a 7526A>G mutation in the MT-TD gene exhibited progressively worsening symptoms, including exercise intolerance, elevated creatine kinase levels, muscle pain, and general malaise following sustained physical activity. Another patient with a 7543A>G mutation also presented with symptoms consistent with the disease.
